clips.start_words: This first started, there was a story
clips.caption:
A Harvard class was asked who had a goal. Seventy percent said yes.

Only three percent had written it down. Fifteen years later, researchers found that same three percent — not seventy, just three — had built more wealth than the other ninety-seven combined.

Writing it down isn't a productivity trick. It's the one variable researchers could actually isolate between the ones who got there and the ones who just talked about it.

Comment RISE and I'll send you how to do it properly.

clips.end_words: He knew exactly what he wanted
clips.caption:
Ask someone their name and they answer instantly. Ask them what they want, and most people go quiet.

That silence is the whole problem. Not the economy, not bad luck — just the absence of a specific, measurable thing to aim at. Andrew Carnegie didn't want to be "successful." He wanted to be the largest steel producer in the world, and he could say it without blinking, in any interview, at any time.

You can't hit a target you've never actually named. "More money" isn't a target. A number is.
